title: Prompting Productive Effort
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans considers what teachers should say to students before an assessment, starting from the demoralising case of a student who works hard and gets a result that does not reflect it. He names three avoidable causes: studying the wrong content, using an inefficient method, and misunderstanding what the assessment rewards. Misdirected effort matters because it damages motivation, yields weak evidence of attainment and effort, and wastes a chance to strengthen retrieval. On content, he argues that the right amount of disclosure depends on the assessment's purpose, and that motivation follows a hill-shaped curve: tell students enough to believe effort can change the outcome, but not so much that they feel they already know enough. On form, the type of test items signals what it means to be good at a subject, so teachers should be truthful about format while encouraging productive study. On preparation, assessments are a chance to show students that effective study leads to success, which builds belief through experience.
points: Wasted effort comes from three sources: wrong focus, inefficient method, and misjudging what the test rewards, all of which a teacher can reduce with better pre-assessment guidance.
The optimal amount of information about test content depends on whether the aim is valid inference about a broad domain or motivating study of a narrow topic.
Motivation is hill-shaped, so students need enough information to believe effort will pay off without being reassured they already know enough.
Test format teaches students what a subject is about, so vocabulary-only or essay-only assessment can distort what students think mastery means.
Teachers build credibility for productive study behaviours over time by letting students experience that those behaviours lead to better results.
quotes: This has probably happened for one of three reasons. Firstly, the student has focused on the wrong thing, such as revising content which does not appear on a test. Secondly, their approach is inefficient, meaning the time spent has little impact on their knowledge and skill.

Poor performance due to misguided effort matters because it will affect a student’s future motivation. It also matters because their performance will provide weak information about what the student is capable of or how hard they have worked, possibly leading to invalid inferences about both attainment and effort.

The motivational curve is hill-shaped in that the optimal strategy is to tell students enough for them to believe that their efforts can change the outcome, but not so much as to reassure them that they already know enough.

The form of assessments – the type of test items and the structure of assessments – signal to students information about the subject’s knowledge architecture and what it means to be good at the subject.

For example, if we were to give nothing but vocabulary tests in French, students may come to believe that learning vocabulary is what the subject is about. Similarly, if a History teacher only ever set essays, students may come to believe that being good at writing essays is a proxy for what it means to be good at the subject of History.

The risk is that by providing too much information students will study for the test, not to achieve deeper understanding. We cannot lie to students about the form of the test, but we can avoid being too explicit.
It is not enough for study to improve the chance of success, students must also believe that this is so. This belief comes from experience.
